w: What's tested Why the female tract develops by default How a follicle grows and releases its egg How the follicle makes estrogen: two cells, two hormones Who controls whom: GnRH, FSH, LH, estrogen, progesterone, inhibin The 28-day cycle: what's high when, and what the uterus is doing Menopause and missed periods Dr. Madison's two biggest hints in class: compare the follicular and luteal phases ("high yield for exam"), and know who responds to what in the follicle, FSH on granulosa cells and LH on theca cells ("very important slide"). The default pathway No Y chromosome means no testes. No testes means two missing hormones. No AMH, so the Müllerian ducts form. No testosterone, so the Wolffian ducts fade away. Nothing from the ovary is needed. Memory hook: anti-Müllerian hormone is named for the duct it removes, so with no AMH the Müllerian ducts stay. Testosterone is what keeps the Wolffian ducts alive. No DHT either, so the outside parts form as female. The Müllerian ducts become the tubes and the uterus. The ovary The follicles live in the cortex. The vessels run through the medulla and hilum. The ovary isn't attached to the tube: the fimbriae sweep the egg in. Fertilization happens in the tube. The control chain Hypothalamus makes GnRH. GnRH goes down the portal system to the anterior pituitary. The pituitary makes FSH and LH. They make the ovary produce estrogen and inhibin. GnRH neurons don't listen to stress, food or inflammation directly. KNDy neurons (K for kisspeptin) pass those messages on. That is how stress or poor nutrition can change the cycle. Leptin, a sign there's enough fuel, turns GnRH up. Stress, inflammation, low blood sugar and prolactin turn it down. The two levels are always balancing each other. The lecture calls it a dynamic equilibrium: pituitary hormones push the ovary, and ovarian hormones push back. Feedback: the big idea Progesterone: always a brake. Inhibin: a brake on FSH only. That's why FSH barely rises at midcycle while LH surges. Estrogen: a brake at normal levels, but above about 200 picograms per milliliter it flips to an accelerator. The pituitary gets extra sensitive to GnRH and LH surges. That flip is positive feedback. It is why women cycle and men don't. Men only have the brakes, so their hormones stay level. Picture it as a car. For most of the month estrogen keeps a foot on the brake. Near day 14, estrogen climbs past 200 and the same hormone floors the gas: LH shoots up and the follicle bursts. After ovulation, progesterone takes over the brake for the second half. Two cells, two hormones Theca cells: LH. They make testosterone. LH speeds up cholesterol desmolase (P450scc), the slow step. They have no aromatase. Like Leydig cells. Granulosa cells: FSH. They use aromatase to turn that testosterone into estrogen. Like Sertoli cells. Memory hook: T for theca, T for testosterone. Granulosa does the finishing step. Cholesterol desmolase and aromatase are the only two enzymes he said to know. At midcycle, granulosa cells add LH receptors to keep making estrogen and to get ready to become the corpus luteum. Two quick tests of the idea. Block LH: theca cells stop making testosterone, so there is nothing to convert, and estrogen falls. Block FSH: testosterone is still made, but aromatase isn't switched on, so it never becomes estradiol. Either way, estrogen drops. Three estrogens Estradiol: the ovary's main one. Estrone: menopause. Made from adrenal DHEA. Much weaker than estradiol. Estriol: pregnancy. Made in the placenta from a fetal precursor. Hook: estrone has "one", the last one standing after menopause. Estriol has "tri", for the three parts of a pregnancy that make it: mom, baby and placenta. A follicle's life Primordial: waits until puberty, up to 13 to 50 years. Primary: one layer of granulosa cells, which get FSH receptors. Secondary: many granulosa layers plus a theca. The theca interna gets LH receptors. Graafian: a fluid-filled antrum. A few start each cycle; one becomes dominant. Corpus luteum: what's left after rupture. Mostly granulosa cells. Lasts about 14 days, then scars into the corpus albicans unless a pregnancy takes over. Heads up: the histology lecture uses different names for the same steps. It calls the many-layer stage a late primary follicle, and the follicle with an antrum a secondary follicle. Learn the order; it is the same in both. Dr. Madison said not to worry about the in-between names: just know that one follicle becomes dominant and releases the egg, and the rest fade. The egg finishes its first meiotic division by ovulation and its second in the fallopian tube. Until the LH surge, an inhibitor in the follicle (OMI, oocyte maturation inhibitor) keeps it paused. The cycle in four beats Days 0 to 14, follicular, "proliferative": estrogen rises. The lining grows, its arteries lengthen, cervical mucus is watery and stretchy. The goal: help sperm reach the egg. Day 14, midcycle: estrogen passes 200, LH surges, and FSH rises a little too (inhibin keeps it small). The egg comes out 24 to 36 hours after the surge. Collagenases weaken the wall; prostaglandins boost blood flow. Days 14 to 28, luteal, "secretory": the corpus luteum makes progesterone. The lining stops proliferating and gets secretory, full of vessels and stocked with glycogen. Mucus turns thick. Body temperature rises slightly. The goal: get ready for implantation. Day 28, menses: the corpus luteum fades, estrogen and progesterone crash, the lining sheds. Ovulation is about 14 days before the next period. In a 28-day cycle that is day 14. In a 32-day cycle, it is about day 18. The second half stays about the same, because the corpus luteum lasts about 14 days. Heads up: the histology lecture counts the days by the uterus instead. Menstrual days 1 to 5, proliferative days 5 to 14, secretory days 15 to 28. Same cycle, same ovulation at about day 14. Quick check: on day 21, which hormone is in charge? Progesterone, from the corpus luteum. On day 10? Estrogen, from the growing follicles, still acting as a brake. Uterus cheat sheet Estrogen grows the lining and contracts the muscle. Progesterone sustains the lining, adds vessels and relaxes the muscle. The endometrium is where an embryo implants. The myometrium is the muscle, for delivery. He said he won't test the slide on estrogen's and progesterone's whole-body effects (skin, memory, gut, heart). Menopause The follicles are gone (atresia, programmed cell death). They had been dwindling for years. No follicles means no estradiol and no inhibin, so no brakes. GnRH, LH and FSH all go up. Rising GnRH has been linked to hot flashes (still being researched, he said). Estrone, made from adrenal DHEA, becomes the main estrogen. Expect a thinner vaginal lining, less vaginal fluid, smaller breasts and faster bone loss. The pattern to recognize: high FSH and LH with low estradiol. Don't confuse it with midcycle, where LH is high because estradiol is high. Missed periods Amenorrhea means no periods. Primary: they never started. Secondary: they started, then stopped. The slide's causes of secondary amenorrhea: pregnancy, lactation, menopause and high prolactin. Turner syndrome (an X partly or completely lost, malformed ovaries) is on the slide as a disorder of sexual differentiation; in class it was his example of primary amenorrhea. High prolactin turns GnRH down, which is how breastfeeding or a prolactin-secreting tumor stops periods. For a case: periods that stopped, a negative pregnancy test, no nursing, normal FSH and high prolactin point to hyperprolactinemia. High FSH would point to menopause instead. Read the labs High progesterone, low FSH and LH: luteal phase. Estradiol over 200 and LH shooting up: about to ovulate. High FSH and LH, low estradiol: menopause. Low progesterone on day 21 and no LH surge: no ovulation, so no corpus luteum. Why no ovulation? Estradiol never got past 200, so it never flipped to the gas pedal. No LH surge, no rupture, no corpus luteum, no progesterone.
